extracted.intended_audience: people organizing or participating in online math exposition (creators of math explainers, contest judges, SoME1 participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reflections on designing and running a contest (SoME1) to evaluate online math explainers (videos, blog posts, games, etc.), including peer-review logistics, fairness concerns, and the qualities that make for excellent math exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessability within 10 minutes
rubrics_metrics.description: We set no explicit constraints on the length of entries, but we did say that someone judging it should be able to assess its quality within 10 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an initial-pass constraint to keep throughput manageable. In practice, judges may spend more time on finalists and write personalized feedback; the 10-minute rule is for first-pass evaluations only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review contribution requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be considered for the final judgement, participants needed to contribute 1 hour to the peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The expected experience: look at two pieces (A and B) and decide which is better according to the contest principles, then continue with further pairwise comparisons. This requirement both supplies reviewer labor and gives participants stake in the ranking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the four principles for comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons between pieces were to be made 'according to the four principles laid out in the original announcement of the event.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges should use those shared principles as the evaluation rubric when making pairwise choices. (The post references these principles but does not reprint them — they are in the original announcement.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairwise ranking via Gavel (Bradley–Terry)
rubrics_metrics.description: We used Gavel, based on the Bradley–Terry algorithm, to assign rankings from pairwise selections; the system also models judge trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical notes: ~13,000 comparisons were made; after ~7,000 the top-100 list stabilized, giving some assurance rankings are not random. The algorithm attempts to be smart about which pairs to show and to estimate both item ranks and judge reliability. Be aware of failure modes (e.g., an item that should be top-5 could be pushed below top-100 by inefficiencies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying solely on upvotes/likes
rubrics_metrics.description: Using something like number of up-votes or likes would make for an easy first-pass filter, but runs the risk of punishing more niche content with a very deliberate and specific target audience, or which has not yet built up any kind of audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popularity metrics are convenient but biased toward already-visible or broadly appealing work. Use pairwise quality-focused comparisons instead of raw popularity when the goal is to surface meaningful or niche lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor meaningful lessons over judgeability
rubrics_metrics.description: There was a tension between making the contest easy to judge and having people produce lessons that would be genuinely helpful to people; the organizers leaned toward encouraging meaningful lessons even if that made judging harder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing evaluation rules, accept some additional judging difficulty if it preserves the event's goal of encouraging substantive, helpful explanations rather than optimizing only for easy evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of format bias (video vs. non-video)
rubrics_metrics.description: A systematic bias occurred where some people thought it was a contest only for videos and downvoted non-video entries accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let the platform of announcement (e.g., YouTube) dictate which formats are judged favorably. Manually audit underrepresented formats (the organizers reviewed many non-video entries that hadn't bubbled up) to mitigate this bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of excellent math exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities like clarity, strong motivation, compelling choices of topic matter, and non-obvious insights represent what makes for excellent math exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these qualities as evaluative dimensions when judging: clarity of explanation, how well the piece motivates the topic, the interest/aptitude of the chosen topic, and whether the work reveals non-obvious insights or surprising connections. Examples of winners illustrate these qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solid idea plus engaging explanation outweighs perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: None were perfect; the organizer emphasizes that you shouldn't be worried about a need for it to be excellent in all respects. As long as it's a solid idea, with an engaging explanation, people will resonate with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't penalize minor production or stylistic flaws if the core idea and the explanation engage and communicate well. Value substance and resonance over technical perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: High initial threshold for 'likely best' shortlist
rubrics_metrics.description: For a second-pass shortlist the organizer used a spreadsheet column asking 'is this likely going to be one of the best?', yes or no, and set a very high bar for answering 'yes' so the second pass had a small handful to choose between.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When narrowing finalists, apply a strict yes/no filter to keep the candidate pool small and manageable for deeper review. Be aware this can lead to many 'probably' or 'maybe' labels which are less useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize apples-to-oranges comparison difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing submissions felt apples-to-oranges: one might be great for topic choice, another for a visual intuition, another for a surprising application; it's inherently subjective and difficult to compare directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design judging procedures that accept heterogeneity in why entries succeed. Consider multi-dimensional notes rather than forcing a single scalar comparison, and recognize the conceptual absurdity of a single winner across very different strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation curation should not imply ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing lists (e.g., all entries or a playlist), mild curation was applied to put favored entries toward the top, but the order should not be interpreted as a ranking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you mildly curate a presented list, explicitly state that ordering is not a ranking to avoid misleading readers; reserve formal rankings for algorithmic or judge-produced lists.
